Ad Network vs Ad Exchange vs DSP: The Middlemen

By lowob · 9 July 2026 · 4-minute read · Distribution

Ad networks bundle and resell publisher inventory with little visibility, ad exchanges run real-time auctions, and DSPs are the software buyers use to bid. The DSP is where control lives. Buyers should know which one they are paying, what it charges and what it lets them see.

Between a company's media budget and the page where its ad appears sit several intermediaries with overlapping names. Three of them account for most of the confusion: ad networks, ad exchanges, and demand-side platforms. Knowing which one you are dealing with tells you what you are paying for and what you can control.

Ad networks

An ad network aggregates inventory from many publishers, packages it, and sells it to advertisers. The network buys or represents the publishers' ad space, often at a negotiated rate, and resells it, usually as bundles by category, audience, or format. The advertiser deals with the network's sales team or interface; the network decides where the ads run within the bundle.

Networks are the oldest model and the simplest to buy from. Their weakness is opacity: the advertiser rarely sees exactly which sites ran the ads, at what cost to the network, or how much of the budget reached the publisher. The network's margin is the difference between what it charges and what it pays, and the advertiser does not see it.

Networks still matter, particularly in specialized verticals and in regions and categories the large platforms do not serve well, including some restricted categories that vertical networks were built to carry.

Ad exchanges

An ad exchange is a marketplace where ad impressions are auctioned in real time. Publishers, usually through a supply-side platform, offer impressions to the exchange; buyers, through demand-side platforms, bid on them. The exchange runs the auction and takes a fee, typically a percentage of the winning bid.

Advertisers do not usually deal with an exchange directly. They reach it through a DSP. The exchange is infrastructure, and the practical questions about it are which exchanges a DSP is connected to, what fees each charges, and how well each polices fraud and low-quality inventory.

Demand-side platforms

A DSP is the software an advertiser or its agency uses to buy programmatically: to define audiences, set budgets and bid rules, upload creative, connect to exchanges, apply verification, and report. The DSP charges a platform fee, typically a percentage of media spent through it, plus fees for data and verification features.

The DSP is where control lives. Inclusion lists, verification standards, frequency caps, and optimization goals are set here. A buyer who does not set them accepts the DSP's defaults, and the defaults favor volume.

The money, end to end

An advertiser's dollar spent programmatically passes through the DSP fee, data fees, verification fees, the exchange fee, the supply-side platform fee, and, if there is one, an agency fee, before reaching the publisher. Industry studies have found publishers receive roughly half of what the advertiser spent, with a portion of the rest unaccounted for. Each intermediary is providing a service. The question for a buyer is whether it knows what each one charged.

Which one you are dealing with

If a salesperson sells you a bundle of sites and you do not see the auction, that is a network. If you or your desk operates software that bids on impressions across many sources, that is a DSP, and behind it are exchanges. If a partner "has access to premium inventory" but cannot show you the placements, the fees, and the rejection rate, you do not yet know which one you are dealing with, and you should find out before the next invoice.

Networks bundle and resell inventory opaquely; exchanges run the auctions; DSPs are the software buyers use to bid, and where control lives. Know which one you are paying, what it charges, and what it lets you see.

lowob takeaways

  • Ad networks resell bundled inventory, and the advertiser rarely sees which sites ran the ads or the network's margin.
  • Advertisers usually reach exchanges through a DSP rather than dealing with them directly.
  • Industry studies have found publishers receive roughly half of what advertisers spend programmatically.
